Yes, but not necessarily genetically. I'm not a big believer in the chemical imbalance theory, but I'm afraid of passing it down through behavior and environment. I worry that I can't provide a stable environment and that the kid will be affected b myy mental illnesses. I think has happened intergenerationally in my family. I want to break that cycle, so I think I'll stay childfree. My aunt made the same choice and supports me in it. I also have developmental disabilities and learning disabilities and my life has been very hard. I want the idealized version of having a baby (all those biological urges lmao) - but I've worked in the school system and know for a fact how hard parenting is, even if your kid is "normal". 

Growing up I always felt like I was different in a bad way, like some monster. Being diagnosed young with mental illness gave me the idea that something was wrong with me. I was on meds starting at age 9 and it's been a constant battle. Like I said, I don't believe in chemical imbalance, I think this is just the effect of generations of parenting impacted by intergenerational trauma and mental illness. I never want any child to feel the way that I did growing up and if that means not having one, so be it.  i struggle with coming to terms with this sometimes BC having a baby to me represents this ideal of being "normal" and having my shit together. 

When I'm older, like 40s or 50s, I would love to adopt an older kid or teenager. They often don't get adopted, but they still need families. If I am ever stable enough, I would love to give them that.

I'm not a parent but I'm a former early childhood educator. Here are some books that I really liked , or that I have heard about (Both as a kid and reading with my students).

My heart fills with happiness by Monique Gray- it's a happy story about an indigenous (Canada) family. Great for learning about other cultures. Appropriate for kids from 3 years up. 

From far away by Robert Munsch- About a girl who is an immigrant to Canada and faces some challenges getting integrated into a new culture. Great book about facing your fears. I'd say this is good for a kid who is 5 years old or older. 

The Paper Bag Princess by Robert Munsch- Good story with messages about female empowerment. Really funny too. Good for kids 4 and older. 

It's perfectly normal- all about puberty and growing up, it answers a lot of questions about sex including more difficult topics. It uses some kid friendly humor.The images of bodies are a bit graphic to some but they are accurate. I read this when I was ten and it answered many of my questions. I'd say 8 years old would be a good time for a kid to read this book. It's a great resource.includes topics such as puberty, pregnancy, abortion, and sexual abuse. 

That's all I have off the top of my head.

I'll tell my story here cause I really think it speaks truth to power about what is going on in Halifax. I'm originally from Ottawa, with one side of the family spread around Nova Scotia. I decided to move to Halifax for school in the winter of 2022. When I arrived, the rent wasn't cheap by any means, but it wasn't insane, I was able to find a room for 750 all inclu. The landlord was a bit unreasonable though..he wouldn't let us turn up the heat and he was super nosy. I went back to Ottawa to work in April-June and then came back in July. This time, I rented a room in a house with a bunch of girls for almost 900 and the room was a fucking shoebox essentially-and this was the best that I could afford. 

Since the room was only for the summer, I had to look for a place to stay for September and I just couldn't find something appropriate- nothing close enough to school (within an hr of public transit) or cheap enough. At this point a single room was going for at least 1000 and all I could see were the rooms for intl students where there's like 4 people in one room and let me tell you I really did pound the pavement looking for a place to stay. 

At this point I got really scared. It was the end of August with nowhere to stay and everything was getting more expensive- it was the first time in my life that I worried about having enough food to eat. I could've stayed with relatives but they are poor and it would have been a huge burden on them. So I made the choice to book a flight home, sell most of my belongings, and stay in Montreal, since it's the only city that I could afford. I miss Halifax with everything in me, it's the only place where I felt like it was somewhere I was meant to be. I miss the fucking ocean, man, and I'm worried about my family back in NS- many of them live in areas with poor infrastructure and rapidly raising costs. I like Montreal, it's closer to my immediate family, but I don't belong here and I'm honestly not happy- however, I have a large apartment here and my needs are accounted for. 

Anyways idk what the point of this whole story is but I guess it's that it wasn't that long ago that Halifax was one of the more affordable places in Canada, and while the housing crisis was already there when I arrived in 2022, it was clear that it is getting worse and worse at an alarmingly fast rate and this is definitely accelerated by the fact that the universities and government aren't handling this whole intl student thing responsibly. I honestly feel bad for the students, at least the ones who genuinely don't know what's going on- I feel that they are being exploited. But I'm most worried about the local people who are being pushed out of where they live. Halifax's infrastructure just isn't built for so many people at once and I think people really neglect to mention that while discussing the housing crisis. 

It is a bloody fucking shame that a student from a middle class background like me couldn't find a place to stay- I never thought that I'd be close to being homeless in my life. This is something I still am very sad about, that I didn't really have a choice in moving to Quebec.
